title: Resource Modeling & HTTP Semantics
objectives: Model endpoints as noun resources addressed by standard HTTP methods
Apply method semantics: safety, idempotency, and retry behavior
Choose correct status codes and design non-CRUD actions as subresources
body:
# Resource Modeling & HTTP Semantics

## The problem
You must expose an orders system over HTTP. Do you create `POST /createOrder`? `POST /orders/new`? `PUT /orders/{id}`? Endpoints designed as remote procedure calls squander the protocol: every client must learn bespoke vocabulary, caches and proxies cannot help you, and status codes degenerate into 200-with-an-error-field. Resource modeling fixes this by making URLs nouns and letting HTTP verbs carry the meaning.

## Nouns, not verbs
A resource is a thing the system manages; a URL names it; the method says what happens to it:

```text
GET    /orders            list the collection
POST   /orders            create a new order
GET    /orders/42         read one order
PUT    /orders/42         replace order 42 (full representation)
PATCH  /orders/42         partially update order 42
DELETE /orders/42         remove order 42
GET    /orders/42/items   nested collection
```

## Method semantics clients rely on
- GET/HEAD: safe - no observable state change, and cacheable.
- PUT: idempotent - repeating it leaves the same state, so retries are safe.
- DELETE: idempotent - the second call still yields 204/404 with no extra effect.
- POST: neither safe nor idempotent - retries need an idempotency key.

## Status codes are part of the contract
- `201 Created` plus `Location: /orders/43` after a successful POST.
- `400` for malformed syntax vs `422` for well-formed but semantically invalid input.
- `401` who are you vs `403` I know who you are, and still no.
- `404` for missing resources, `409` for conflicting state (duplicates).
- `429` with `Retry-After` for throttling.

## Design decisions & tradeoffs
- Nested routes (`/orders/42/items`) express ownership but get deep fast; beyond two levels, link by id instead.
- Actions that are not CRUD (`cancel`, `refund`): either PATCH a state field, or add a subresource `POST /orders/42/cancellation`. Prefer the subresource when the action is auditable and has its own lifecycle.
- Bulk operations: an explicit `POST /orders/batch` contract, not comma-joined id hacks.

## Decision framework
1. Can you name it as a noun with an id? -> resource plus standard verbs.
2. Is the operation a state transition? -> PATCH a field, or POST a subresource - whichever future-you can audit.
3. Would a retry duplicate the effect? -> require an idempotency key.

## Best practices
- Use plural collection names (`/orders`, never `/order`).
- Return the created representation and a Location header from POST.
- Keep URLs opaque: ids in, ids out; clients should never parse meaning out of them.
- Use a problem-details style error body so failures stay machine-readable.

## Common mistakes
- `GET /deleteOrder?id=42`: an unsafe method with side effects that crawlers and prefetchers will trigger.
- Returning `200 OK` with an error body - it breaks generic clients and monitoring that counts status codes.
- Deep nesting like `/users/7/orders/42/items/9/reviews/3`; reference top-level ids instead.
- Verbs in URLs (`/getUsers`) duplicating what the method already says.

examples.name: orders-crud.sh
examples.code:
# Create
curl -i -X POST https://api.example.com/orders \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"sku":"A1","qty":2}'
# HTTP/1.1 201 Created
# Location: /orders/43

# Idempotent replace (safe to retry)
curl -i -X PUT https://api.example.com/orders/43 \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"sku":"A1","qty":3}'
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK

# Wrong method on a collection
curl -i -X DELETE https://api.example.com/orders
# HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
# Allow: GET, POST

exercise.prompt: Implement badRoutes(routes): each route is a string like "POST /createOrder". Return the routes whose path embeds a verb (create, get, delete, update, add, new) - the RPC-style paths that duplicate what the HTTP method should express.
hints: Split each route into method and path; only inspect the path.
Lowercase the path and test it against a list of verb substrings.
DELETE /orders/42 is fine - delete appears as the method, not in the path.

questions.prompt: Which request is idempotent and therefore safe to retry after a timeout?
questions.explanation: PUT replaces the resource's state with the same payload every time, so retries converge; POST can create duplicates and PATCH is not guaranteed idempotent.

questions.prompt: The client is authenticated but lacks permission for this order. Correct status?
questions.explanation: 401 means the caller's identity is unknown or unverified; 403 means identity is known but access is denied.

questions.prompt: Best response for a successful collection POST that created /orders/43?
questions.explanation: 201 signals a new resource was created, and Location tells the client where to find it.
